newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong's Tung reshuffles government.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Tung reshuffles government.

text.p: Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa on Monday carried out his first government reshuffle since the former British colony was handed back to China four weeks ago.
The widely expected reshuffle was announced in a government statement. It entailed no dramatic changes and there were no obvious political casualties.
Transport Secretary Gordon Siu will become head of Chief Executive Tung's think tank, the Central Policy Unit, in a move predicted by sources close to the government.
Constitutional Affairs Secretary Nicholas Ng will replace Siu as transport policy chief. Ng's position will be filled by Home Affairs Secretary Michael Suen.
"This is not a big shake-up," a political analyst said. "It's more of a sideways shuffle."
The reshuffle was the first to go through a new system of prior approval by Beijing.
Technically, Hong Kong cabinet appointments are now made by the communist Chinese government based on nominations by Tung. Before July 1 appointments were made by a British colonial governor.
The top three officials in the government -- Chief Administrative Secretary Anson Chan, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang and Security Secretary Peter Lai -- were not affected.

Chan, Tung's deputy and head of the 180,000-strong Civil Service, said in the statement that the reshuffled officials "are all capable and experienced officers who are well qualified for their new appointments".
"Both the Chief Executive and I are confident that they will bring a wealth of experience and strong leadership to the new offices they are about to take up," Chan said.
Hong Kong's top tier of government officials are roughly equivalent to cabinet ministers, but they are unelected civil servants, not politicians.
Hong Kong, a thriving capitalist outpost of 6.4 million people, reverted to Beijing's control as a special Chinese region on July 1, ending 156 years of British colonial rule.
Tung, chosen by Beijing, reappointed all but one of the top 14 colonial-era officials including Chan and Tsang, in a move widely applauded in Hong Kong and overseas.
